title: Hidden Airtag reveals Amazon is trashing rare books to train AI
gist: An Airtag hidden in a rare book by a bookseller traced a bulk order to an Amazon AI-training facility in Las Vegas (team VGT3) that destructively scans rare books for frontier-model training data, confirming booksellers' suspicions and highlighting the scramble for unique, ISBN-catalogued text amid a training-data shortage.

insights.claim: Amazon is developing frontier AI models that require massive unique training data, and workers reported the Las Vegas scanning facility ran low on and at one point completely ran out of books earlier this year, fearing shutdown.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Confirms acute scarcity of high-quality unique text for frontier training—a strategic bottleneck driving unusual data-sourcing behavior.
insights.locator: Further, it seems that Amazon needed a new source

insights.claim: Amazon workers were trained to scan barcodes or ISBNs before scanning books, supporting booksellers' theory that AI firms are methodically working through the global ISBN list to capture every printed book.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Implies a systematic, exhaustive text-acquisition strategy—signal for the scale of the data land-grab underpinning model competitiveness.

insights.claim: Rivals Anthropic and xAI have publicly said they do not train on rare or antique books, making destructively scanned rare text a potential differentiating data source for Amazon versus Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Data provenance is becoming a competitive and reputational battleground among AI labs.
insights.locator: However, Amazon is developing what it considers frontier AI models

insights.claim: Amazon declined to comment on the AI-training angle, using services that mask its identity as a buyer and providing only a generic statement about purchasing books through commercial channels.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Corporate opacity around training data reflects legal and reputational risk that could invite regulation or litigation.
insights.quote: Amazon purchases books through commercial channels to help develop and improve the products and services our customers use

insights.claim: Destructive book scanning has drawn strong backlash, with critic Michael Burry reportedly calling it 'evil incarnate' and booksellers warning that potentially unique surviving editions could be destroyed.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Reputational risk and cultural-heritage concerns could pressure AI firms toward transparency or non-destructive methods.
